Disputing
dĭs-pūt'ĭng
n. and part. (reasoning, debating, contending in argument; rendering Greek suzeteo, zetesis, and dialegomai)
Latin disputare, from dis-, apart, and putare, to reckon — to reckon a matter out. The Authorized Version uses the word both for holy reasoning from the Scriptures and for the wrangling of hardened men.

Biblical Definition

Luke reports both kinds within a few chapters. The synagogue of the Libertines rose up “disputing with Stephen” (Act 6:9), and when they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake they suborned false witnesses instead — disputing that ends in murder because it never intended to be persuaded. At Jerusalem, “when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up” (Act 15:7), and the disputing was the honest labour of a council that then reached a settled judgment. At Ephesus Paul went into the synagogue and spake boldly for three months, “disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God” (Act 19:8), and when divers were hardened he separated the disciples and continued “disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus” (Act 19:9). The Greek there is dialegomai — to reason through a matter — and Luke plainly counts it apostolic work. Two years of daily reasoning is how all Asia heard the word. The dictionary therefore refuses to make argument itself the villain. Paul reasoned; Stephen reasoned; the council reasoned. What Scripture condemns is the disputing that has already decided, and the disputing about nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines disputing as the act of contending in argument; controversy in words; the reasoning or arguing of contending parties.

expand to see more

DISPUTING, ppr. Contending by words or arguments; controverting; debating.

DISPUTING, n. The act of contending in words; controversy; altercation.

DISPUTE, v.i. To contend in argument; to reason or argue in opposition; to debate; to alter cate.

Key Scripture

Act 6:9 — "Then there arose certain of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia, disputing with Stephen."

Act 19:8 — "And he went into the synagogue, and spake boldly for the space of three months, disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God."

Php 2:14 — "Do all things without murmurings and disputings:"

Modern Corruption

Two errors stand on either side of this word: the church that will not reason at all because argument feels unkind, and the church that reasons ceaselessly and never arrives at a judgment.

expand to see more

A common modern instinct treats all argument as a failure of love, and quotes Philippians 2:14 — do all things without murmurings and disputings — to close every doctrinal question before it opens. But Paul who wrote that verse is the same Paul who disputed daily for two years in the school of Tyrannus, and Philippians 2:14 is about the grumbling of a congregation with one another, not about reasoning from the Scriptures with the lost. The opposite error is just as real and rather more common among those most careful about doctrine: a disputing that never terminates. Acts 15 shows the pattern Scripture blesses. There was much disputing, and then Peter rose up, and then James gave sentence, and then the church wrote it down and sent it out. Debate served a decision. The corruption is debate as a permanent condition — the conference, the podcast, the endless thread, in which no question is ever closed because closing it would end the discussion, and the discussion has become the product. Paul reasoned in order to persuade. The measure of his disputing was in Acts 19:10: all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek suzeteo (G4802), to search together, to dispute; zetesis (G2214), a questioning or debate; dialegomai (G1256), to reason through, to discourse; dialogismos (G1261), inward reasoning or murmuring.

expand to see more

Greek suzeteo (G4802) — to search or reason together, and so to dispute; the synagogue against Stephen, and the scribes against the disciples; Acts 6:9, Mark 9:14.

Greek dialegomai (G1256) — to reason, to discourse, to argue a case; Paul's regular method in synagogue and school; Acts 17:2, 19:8-9.

Greek dialogismos (G1261) — reasonings, disputings of the heart; the murmuring Paul forbids the church; Philippians 2:14, Romans 14:1.

Usage

"“Disputing with Stephen” — argument that could not resist the wisdom, and turned to false witnesses."

"“Disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God” — the apostolic pattern; reasoning aimed at persuasion."

"“Do all things without murmurings and disputings” — the congregational rule, not a ban on reasoning."
